lesson.title: Cash, Crime, and the Speakeasy: Bootlegging in the Prohibition Era
lesson.summary: Prohibition created a massive illegal market for alcohol, and criminal organizations, most famously Al Capone's operation in Chicago, grew rich and powerful supplying it, often with the help of bribed police and politicians.
lesson.body:
Once the Eighteenth Amendment made legal alcohol sales impossible, an illegal industry rushed to fill the gap. Bootleggers, so named from an older term for hiding liquor bottles in one's boot, manufactured moonshine in hidden stills, smuggled whiskey down from Canada, and ran rum in from the Caribbean and from ships anchored just outside U.S. territorial waters, a smuggling route nicknamed Rum Row. This illegal supply chain fed the thousands of speakeasies that had sprung up in cities across the country, and because the entire business operated outside the law, it also operated outside any legal regulation of price, quality, or fair competition, conditions that rewarded whoever was willing to use violence and bribery to control the market.

No one came to symbolize this new criminal landscape more than Al Capone, who built a bootlegging, gambling, and prostitution empire based in Chicago and its suburb of Cicero, Illinois, during the mid 1920s. Capone's organization earned enormous profits and used bribery to keep police and local officials cooperative, while also engaging in brutal violence against rival gangs. The most notorious incident came on February 14, 1929, when men working for Capone dressed as police officers and gunned down seven members of a rival gang led by Bugs Moran in a Chicago garage, an event that became known as the Saint Valentine's Day Massacre and shocked the nation with its brazenness.

Federal agents, including Eliot Ness and his team of Prohibition enforcers known as the Untouchables, worked to raid Capone's breweries and stills, but it was ultimately federal tax investigators, not Prohibition agents, who brought Capone down. Since Capone had never paid taxes on his illegal income, prosecutors convicted him of federal tax evasion in 1931, and he was sentenced to eleven years in prison, a conviction that removed him from power without ever directly punishing him for the bootlegging or violence that had made him famous. Capone's rise and fall illustrated a pattern seen in cities across the country: Prohibition did not eliminate the demand for alcohol, it simply handed control of the supply to whoever was willing to break the law, and the organized crime networks built during this decade often outlasted Prohibition itself, moving into other illegal rackets once the Eighteenth Amendment was finally repealed.
